h1: Meter Socket Replacement in Broward County
intro: The meter socket is the box where the power company's meter plugs into your building, and it takes the full brunt of South Florida weather. Rust streaks under the meter, a cracked or loose enclosure, scorch marks, or a meter that looks tilted are all signs that socket is failing. Left alone, a bad meter socket can arc, overheat, or drop power to the whole property, because everything downstream runs through it. Replacing it is not a job to hand a handyman, and it is not a job to do without the power company: the utility has to disconnect and reconnect the meter, and that must be scheduled and coordinated. We handle that coordination and the permit for you, so it goes smoothly. You are paying for the experience, and for a job priced once and priced right.

definition.heading: What a meter socket is and why it fails
definition.body: The meter socket is the weatherproof enclosure that holds the utility meter and connects the power company's service to your home or building. All of your electricity passes through it, which means when it corrodes or cracks, the whole property is affected. In South Florida it fails for a few predictable reasons: salt air and humidity corrode the metal jaws and lugs inside, decades of heat loosen connections, water finds its way past a cracked cover, and physical damage or a nearby fault can burn the contacts. A failing socket shows up as rust, heat, flickering, or intermittent power. Because the meter itself belongs to the utility, replacing the socket requires coordinating a disconnect and reconnect with the power company, and the work is permitted and inspected. We manage all of it as one clean job.

symptoms.title: Rust and corrosion on the enclosure
symptoms.body: You see rust streaks, pitting, or a chalky buildup on the meter box, especially at the bottom. Salt air and humidity corrode the metal and the connections inside, and corrosion adds heat. A rusted socket is on its way to failing and worth replacing before it does.

symptoms.title: Scorch marks or a burning smell
symptoms.body: Brown scorch marks, melted spots, or a hot plastic smell around the meter mean the connections are arcing or overheating. That is a fire risk at the point where all your power enters. Stop and call, because this is not a wait and see situation.

symptoms.title: The meter looks loose or tilted
symptoms.body: The meter sits crooked in its socket, wobbles, or has visible gaps around it. Loose jaws inside the socket no longer grip the meter blades tightly, which causes arcing and heat. A meter that will not sit square is telling you the socket is worn out.

symptoms.title: Flickering or intermittent power
symptoms.body: The whole property flickers, dims, or briefly loses power for no clear reason. When the trouble affects everything at once, the fault is often right at the service, where a corroded or loose meter socket connection cannot carry the load steadily anymore.

symptoms.title: A cracked or damaged cover
symptoms.body: The meter enclosure is cracked, the cover is broken or missing, or water is getting inside. In our climate an open or cracked socket invites moisture and corrosion straight to the live connections, which speeds failure and creates a hazard.

symptoms.title: The utility red-tagged the meter
symptoms.body: The power company flagged your meter equipment as unsafe or refused to reconnect until it is fixed. When the utility red-tags a socket, it must be replaced by a licensed electrician and inspected before power is restored, and we handle that whole process.

localSections.heading: Salt air, humidity, and aging meter equipment
localSections.body: Nothing on a South Florida property takes more abuse than the meter socket. It hangs outside, exposed to sun, rain, humidity, and, near the coast, salt air that corrodes metal at a pace inland systems never see. Inside the enclosure, the jaws and lugs that grip the meter and carry your entire electrical load are metal, and metal in this climate corrodes, and corrosion adds resistance, and resistance makes heat. On a socket installed in the nineteen seventies or eighties, that slow chemistry has been running for decades. The result is the rust streaks, loose meters, and heat damage we are called out to replace. Because everything the property uses passes through this one point, a corroded socket is not a small cosmetic issue; it is a single point of failure for the whole building. We replace it with equipment rated to survive our conditions, because installing anything less just starts the same countdown over again.

localSections.heading: The utility disconnect and reconnect
localSections.body: A meter socket cannot simply be swapped while it is live, because the utility owns the meter and controls the power feeding into it. Replacing the socket safely means the power company has to disconnect the service, and once the new socket is installed and inspected, reconnect it and reset the meter. That coordination is one of the most important parts of the job and one of the most common places a homeowner or an unlicensed handyman gets stuck. We handle the scheduling with the utility, line up the disconnect and reconnect, and time our work to fit that window so your power is off for the shortest safe period. Because we do this regularly across Broward County, we know how the local process works and how to keep it moving. You do not have to sit on hold with the power company or guess at the sequence; we manage the whole handoff from disconnect to reconnect as part of the job.

localSections.heading: Permitting and inspection in Broward
localSections.body: Meter socket replacement is service-side electrical work, and in Broward County it is permitted and inspected, not something done quietly on the side. That is a good thing for a property owner. A permitted, inspected socket replacement means a licensed contractor did the work to code and an inspector confirmed it, which is exactly the record you want at the point where all your power enters the building. We pull the permit under our own license, coordinate the inspection with the utility reconnect, and we meet the inspector in person rather than sending a stranger. Skipping the permit to save a little time is a false economy: an unpermitted change at the meter can surface as a problem at sale, at refinance, or when an insurance carrier looks closely after a claim. We keep the paperwork clean so the new socket is an asset on the record, not a question mark waiting to be found later.

localSections.heading: What insurance carriers watch
localSections.body: Insurance carriers in South Florida pay close attention to the electrical service, and the meter socket sits right at the front of it. A corroded, scorched, or damaged socket is the kind of visible hazard an inspector or adjuster notices immediately, and it can affect a policy or a claim. If an electrical fire or failure ever traces back to the service equipment, the carrier will want to know whether the socket was replaced by a licensed contractor and whether the work was permitted and inspected. Unpermitted or handyman work at the meter is a red flag that can slow a claim or put coverage at risk. When we replace a socket we do it under our license, coordinate the utility and the permit, and leave documented, inspected work behind. For a property manager, that clean record is part of protecting the owner, and it is the kind of thing that quietly keeps a policy in good standing and a claim moving if one is ever filed.

guide.title: The complete guide to meter socket replacement in South Florida

sections.heading: What the meter socket is and where it sits
sections.body: The meter socket is easy to overlook because it looks like a simple round or square box on an exterior wall with the utility meter plugged into it, but it is one of the most important pieces of equipment on the property. It is the physical junction between the power company's service and your building. The utility's wires feed into it, the meter plugs into a set of metal jaws inside it, and from there every bit of electricity the property uses flows onward to your main breaker or disconnect and then to the panel. Because it sits at that single chokepoint, the condition of the socket affects everything downstream. A healthy socket grips the meter firmly, keeps water out, and carries the full load without heating up. A failing one does the opposite: loose jaws let the meter arc, cracks let moisture in, and corroded connections turn into hot spots. Understanding that the socket is a single point of failure for the whole property is the key to taking its warning signs seriously. When it is struggling, it is not one circuit at risk, it is the entire service.

sections.heading: Why meter sockets fail here more than most places
sections.body: Meter sockets wear out everywhere, but South Florida is especially hard on them, and it helps to understand why so the warning signs make sense. The first factor is corrosion. Humidity is high year round, and near the coast salt rides the air and settles on everything, and both attack the metal parts inside the enclosure. Those metal jaws and lugs are what grip the meter and carry your load, so as they corrode they lose their tight contact and their ability to move current cleanly. The second factor is heat, both from the climate and from the electrical load itself. Corroded and loose connections have higher resistance, and resistance turns into heat every time current flows, so a struggling socket literally cooks itself a little more each day the air conditioning runs. The third factor is age. A great deal of the housing stock here was built decades ago, and much of that original service equipment is still in place, having weathered forty or fifty summers. Add the occasional storm, surge, or physical bump, and you have the recipe for the rusted, scorched, loose sockets we replace regularly. None of it is unusual for this region; it is simply what our climate does to metal over time.

sections.heading: The warning signs worth acting on
sections.body: Because the meter socket is outside and easy to walk past, its warnings often go unnoticed until power is affected, so it is worth knowing what to look for. Rust streaks, pitting, or a chalky white buildup on the enclosure, particularly along the bottom, signal corrosion working on the metal. Brown scorch marks, melted plastic, or a hot smell near the meter are more serious and mean connections are already arcing or overheating; those deserve a call right away. A meter that sits crooked, wobbles, or has gaps around it points to worn jaws that no longer grip the blades tightly, which causes arcing. A cracked or missing cover lets water reach live parts and accelerates the whole process. And whole-property symptoms, flickering, dimming, or brief losses of power that affect everything at once, often trace back to the service and the socket rather than any single circuit inside. Finally, if the utility itself has red-tagged the meter or refused to reconnect until the equipment is fixed, that is a clear instruction that the socket needs licensed replacement. Catching these signs early turns an emergency into a planned, scheduled job, which is easier on everyone and usually easier on the wallet.

sections.heading: How the replacement actually goes
sections.body: A meter socket replacement is a coordinated job with several moving parts, and knowing the sequence takes the mystery out of it. It starts with the assessment: we come out, confirm the socket is truly the problem, and check whether the failure has affected the meter, the service conductors, the main disconnect, or the panel it feeds, because sometimes a bad socket has already damaged what is next to it. Then you get one honest price that includes the utility coordination and the permit. Next comes scheduling, and this is where a licensed contractor earns their keep, because the power company has to disconnect the service before the socket can be safely removed. We arrange that disconnect, and when it is done our in-house crew removes the old socket, installs new weatherproof equipment properly rated for our climate, and makes every connection to code. The work is inspected, and we meet the inspector in person rather than sending someone unfamiliar. Once it passes, the utility reconnects the service and resets the meter, and your power comes back on. Throughout, we plan the timing so the power is off for the shortest safe window, which matters a great deal when tenants are counting on the lights and the air conditioning.

sections.heading: Utility coordination, permitting, and why they matter
sections.body: The two things that separate a proper meter socket replacement from a risky one are utility coordination and permitting, and both are worth understanding. The meter belongs to the power company, not to you, which means no one should be pulling it or working live at the socket without the utility's involvement. The correct process is a scheduled disconnect, the licensed work, an inspection, and then a reconnect. We manage that whole chain so you are not left calling the utility yourself or, worse, tempted to let someone work around it. Permitting is the other half. Service-side work like this is permitted and inspected in Broward County for a reason: it is the front door of your entire electrical system, and the county wants a licensed professional and an independent inspector to confirm it was done right. We pull the permit under our license and we meet the inspector in person. This protects you in ways that are easy to underestimate. A permitted, inspected socket is clean on the record at sale and refinance, it holds up if an insurance carrier ever looks closely, and it means the work carries real accountability. Skipping either step to save a day almost never pays off, because the shortcut tends to reappear as a bigger, costlier problem down the line.

sections.heading: Choosing the right electrician for the job
sections.body: Meter socket replacement is not a job for a general handyman, and choosing the right electrician protects both your property and your wallet. Start with licensing, because service-side work demands it: you want a Florida Certified Electrical Contractor with statewide authority and, here in Broward, a county Master Electrician, so the person doing the work is accountable to the state and knows how the local utility and building department operate. Ask whether the company coordinates the utility disconnect and reconnect and pulls the permit, or whether they expect you to handle that; the honest, experienced answer is that they take care of it as part of the job. Ask whether an in-house crew does the work or a subcontractor you will never see again. Be cautious of anyone who offers to swap a socket without involving the utility or without a permit, because that is a shortcut that can hurt you later. Ghost Crown Electric has run for ten years, holds 286 permitted projects on public record, and stays in the top tier of Florida contractors by permit quality, with our licensed team taking the call, pricing the job, and meeting the inspector in person. When the front door of your electrical system needs work, that kind of accountability is exactly what you want standing behind it, and it is why we price it once and price it right.

sections.heading: What a socket replacement protects, and when to plan it
sections.body: Because the meter socket sits at the single point where all your power enters the building, replacing a failing one protects far more than the box itself. A corroded or overheating socket can damage the meter, the service conductors, the main disconnect, and the panel just downstream of it, so catching the socket before it fails completely often saves the more expensive equipment behind it. That is why the visible warning signs, rust, heat, a loose meter, a cracked cover, are worth acting on early rather than waiting for the whole property to go dark. Timing matters too. A socket that is showing corrosion but still working can be replaced on a planned schedule, coordinated with the utility for a convenient window, rather than as a middle-of-the-night emergency at an after-hours premium. For a landlord or property manager, planning the work means less disruption for tenants and a price you can budget instead of one forced by a crisis. We will always tell you honestly where a socket sits on that curve: whether it is a watch-it situation, a plan-it-soon situation, or a replace-it-now safety issue. There is no fixed calendar for meter equipment the way there is for some maintenance, because the pace depends on exposure to salt air, the age of the equipment, and how hard the service is worked. A socket on a shaded inland wall may last far longer than one taking direct coastal weather. What stays constant is the value of a licensed set of eyes when the signs appear, and of doing the replacement properly when it is due: correct weatherproof equipment, tight connections, the utility coordinated, the permit pulled, and the inspection passed. Done that way, a new socket is a decades-long asset at the front of your electrical system, not a patch that starts corroding again the week after it goes in.

faqs.question: Do I have to deal with the power company myself?
faqs.answer: No. Replacing a meter socket requires the utility to disconnect and reconnect the meter, and we coordinate that for you along with the permit. You do not have to sit on hold or guess at the sequence. We schedule the disconnect, do the work, get it inspected, and arrange the reconnect as one clean job.

faqs.question: How do I know if my meter socket needs replacing?
faqs.answer: Look for rust or corrosion on the box, scorch marks or a hot smell, a meter that sits crooked or loose, a cracked or missing cover, or flickering that affects the whole property. If the utility red-tagged the meter, it must be replaced by a licensed electrician. When in doubt, we come out and confirm what is actually failing before pricing anything.

faqs.question: How long will my power be off?
faqs.answer: Because everything runs through the meter, the power is off during the replacement and the utility disconnect and reconnect. We plan the timing tightly so that window is as short as it safely can be. The exact length depends on the utility scheduling and what we find, which is why we walk you through the plan before the work day.

faqs.question: What does a meter socket replacement cost?
faqs.answer: It is quoted per property, because the price depends on the socket, the condition of the service around it, and the utility coordination involved. The visit starts with the $240 service call, which covers roughly two hours including travel, arrival, and diagnosis. After we assess it, you get one honest number that holds unless we find hidden damage and tell you first.

faqs.question: Can a handyman just swap the socket?
faqs.answer: No, and it is not worth the risk. This is service-side work at the point where all your power enters the building. It requires a licensed electrician, a permit, an inspection, and coordination with the utility to disconnect and reconnect. Unpermitted work at the meter can create real trouble at sale, refinance, or with an insurance carrier later.

faqs.question: Is a corroded meter socket actually dangerous?
faqs.answer: It can be. Corrosion and loose connections raise resistance, resistance makes heat, and heat at the service can lead to arcing or a fire at the one point every circuit depends on. It can also drop or interrupt power to the whole property. Rust alone is a reason to have it looked at, and scorching is a reason to call right away.
